p: Welcome to the primer on brackets and braces. Many people go through school without ever being told plainly what brackets are for. They see curly ones, square ones and round ones, and they feel lost. This primer will put that right, gently, in ten short parts. By the end, brackets will feel like old friends.
Let us start with one simple idea, which is really all brackets are about. Brackets group things together.
## Grouping in everyday language

We group things in speech all the time without noticing. Think of a waiter who asks: would you like tea, or coffee with milk? Does that mean you can have tea, or else coffee-with-milk? Or does it mean you can have tea-or-coffee, and either way it comes with milk? The sentence is ambiguous. In speech, we sort it out by pausing and changing our tone of voice. We might say: tea, pause, or coffee with milk. Or we might say: tea or coffee, pause, with milk.
Written mathematics cannot pause or change its tone of voice. So it uses brackets instead. Brackets are written pauses. They say: this part belongs together.
## Parcels inside a box

Here is a picture to keep. Imagine a brown paper parcel. Inside it are several small things. When you carry the parcel, you carry it as one object, even though there are many things inside. Brackets are the brown paper. Whatever is inside a pair of brackets is wrapped up and treated as one single thing.
## Brackets come in pairs

A bracket always has two halves. There is an opening bracket at the start of the group and a closing bracket at the end. On paper, a round opening bracket curves like the left side of a circle, and the closing bracket curves the other way, like the right side. Together they hug whatever is between them.
When this app reads a formula aloud, it tells you where each bracket opens and closes, in words, in tones, or both. Let us hear a first example.
That was: open bracket, 2 plus 3, close bracket, times 4. The brackets wrap up 2 plus 3 into a parcel. The parcel is worth 5. Then the 5 is multiplied by 4, to give 20.
## Meet the tones
Let us listen to the tones on their own. Here is the opening round bracket. Notice that it rises.
⟦\tone{round-open}⟧
And here is the closing round bracket. Notice that it falls.
⟦\tone{round-close}⟧
Rising to open, falling to close, like a door swinging open and then shut, or like a question and its answer. Here they are together, with a little gap between, as if wrapping something invisible.
⟦\tone{round-open}⟧ ⟦\tone{round-close}⟧
?? Without looking anything up: if you hear a rising tone, then some words, then a falling tone, what has happened?
=> A bracket has opened, some things have been grouped inside it, and the bracket has closed. Everything between the two tones belongs together as one parcel.
## Why bother?

You might ask why we need brackets at all. Could we not just work left to right? The answer is that without brackets, the same string of numbers can mean different things, just like the tea and coffee sentence. Listen to these two.

The first was: open bracket, 2 plus 3, close bracket, times 4. That is 5 times 4, which is 20. The second was: 2 plus, open bracket, 3 times 4, close bracket. That is 2 plus 12, which is 14. The same numbers and the same signs, but different groupings, give different answers. Brackets are how mathematics says exactly what it means.
?? Work out this one in your head: open bracket, 10 minus 4, close bracket, times 2.
=> The parcel is 10 minus 4, which is 6. Then 6 times 2 is 12.
## The golden rule
Here is the golden rule of brackets, which you will hear again and again in this primer. Work out what is inside the brackets first. Treat the inside as one thing. Then carry on with the rest.
In the next part, we will meet the question of what to do first when there are no brackets at all, which is the famous order of operations, known in British schools as BIDMAS or BODMAS.

In part one we learned that brackets say which part to do first. But what happens when there are no brackets? Mathematicians around the world have agreed a set of rules for which operations come first. It is called the order of operations. In Britain, children learn it with a memory word: BIDMAS, or in some schools, BODMAS.
## The word BIDMAS
BIDMAS stands for:
B for Brackets. I for Indices, which are powers such as squared. D for Division. M for Multiplication. A for Addition. S for Subtraction.
BODMAS is exactly the same, except that the O stands for Orders, an older word for powers. Some people say it stands for Of, as in a half of something. Either way, the rules are the same.
## A story to remember it by
Imagine a royal kitchen preparing a banquet. Each kind of operation is a member of staff, and they have a strict order of rank.
The Brackets are the royal family. Whatever they want is done first, before anything else, without question.
The Indices, the powers, are the dukes and duchesses. They come next.

Division and Multiplication are the two head chefs. They are equal in rank. Neither outranks the other. So when both are waiting, they simply take turns in the order they arrive, reading from left to right.
Addition and Subtraction are the two kitchen porters. They are also equal in rank to each other, and they also take turns, left to right. But they always wait until the head chefs have finished.
## The famous example
Here is the example that starts arguments on the internet.
⟦2+3\times 4⟧

That was: 2 plus 3 times 4. If you simply work left to right, you might say 2 plus 3 is 5, times 4 is 20. But the head chef, multiplication, outranks the porter, addition. So multiplication goes first. 3 times 4 is 12. Then 2 plus 12 is 14. The agreed answer is 14.
If we really did want the 2 plus 3 done first, we would have to call in the royal family.
Now, with brackets, the answer is 20.
?? What is 10 minus 2 times 3?
=> Multiplication first: 2 times 3 is 6. Then 10 minus 6 is 4. Not 24.
## Equal partners, left to right

The one part of BIDMAS that confuses many adults is that the letters D and M, and A and S, are not a strict order. Division does not always come before multiplication. They are equal partners, and you take them as they come, from left to right. The same goes for addition and subtraction.
⟦12\div 3\times 2⟧

That was: 12 divided by 3 times 2. Working left to right: 12 divided by 3 is 4, then 4 times 2 is 8. If you did the multiplication first, you would get 12 divided by 6, which is 2, and that would be wrong by the usual convention.
?? Work out 10 minus 3 plus 2, taking addition and subtraction as equal partners from left to right.
=> Left to right: 10 minus 3 is 7, plus 2 is 9. Not 10 minus 5, which would be 5.
## Indices: the dukes and duchesses
Powers come before multiplication. A power is a number multiplied by itself a certain number of times. Three squared means 3 times 3, which is 9.
⟦2\times 3^2⟧
That was: 2 times 3 squared. The power goes first: 3 squared is 9. Then 2 times 9 is 18. Not 6 squared, which would be 36.
## A worked example, step by step
Let us take a longer one and walk through it slowly.
That was: 20 minus, open bracket, 3 plus 1, close bracket, squared, divided by 2.
Step one, brackets: 3 plus 1 is 4. Now we have 20 minus 4 squared divided by 2.
Step two, indices: 4 squared is 16. Now we have 20 minus 16 divided by 2.
Step three, division before subtraction: 16 divided by 2 is 8. Now we have 20 minus 8.
Step four, subtraction: 20 minus 8 is 12.
?? Now try this one yourself: 5 plus 2 times, open bracket, 6 minus 1, close bracket.
=> Brackets first: 6 minus 1 is 5. Then multiplication: 2 times 5 is 10. Then addition: 5 plus 10 is 15.
## Why these rules?

The order of operations is a convention, an agreement, like driving on the left in Britain. It was not handed down from heaven. But it is a very sensible agreement, because it matches how algebra is usually written. When you write 3x plus 2, meaning 3 times x, plus 2, you want the multiplication to stick tightly to the x. Multiplication binds more tightly than addition. The rules simply make that official.
And whenever there is any doubt, the kind thing to do is to add brackets. Brackets never hurt, and they make your meaning crystal clear.

Round brackets are the everyday workhorses of mathematics. In Britain they are simply called brackets. In America they are called parentheses. In this part we will listen to round brackets doing their different jobs.
## Job one: do this first
We already know the first job. Brackets say: do this part first. Let us hear one with a division.
That was: open bracket, 8 plus 4, close bracket, divided by 3. Brackets first: 8 plus 4 is 12. Then 12 divided by 3 is 4.
?? Without the brackets, 8 plus 4 divided by 3 would mean something different. What?
=> Division would go first: 4 divided by 3 is one and a third. Plus 8 is nine and a third. Quite different from 4.
## Job two: hidden multiplication
When a number sits right next to a bracket, with no sign between them, it means multiply. Mathematicians are lazy writers, and they leave out the times sign whenever they can.
That was: 3, open bracket, 4 plus 1, close bracket. It means 3 times the bracket. 4 plus 1 is 5, and 3 times 5 is 15.
Two brackets next to each other also mean multiply.

That was: open bracket, 2 plus 1, close bracket, open bracket, 5 minus 1, close bracket. Notice how you heard the close tone of the first bracket followed straight away by the open tone of the second. It means 3 times 4, which is 12.
?? What is 2, open bracket, 10 minus 7, close bracket?
=> The bracket is 3. Two times 3 is 6.
## Job three: protecting a negative number
Brackets also protect a negative number, keeping its minus sign attached. This matters most with powers. Listen to the difference between these two.
The first was: open bracket, minus 3, close bracket, squared. The whole parcel, minus 3, is squared. Minus 3 times minus 3 is plus 9, because two negatives multiplied make a positive.
The second was: minus 3 squared, with no brackets. By the order of operations, the power goes first, so only the 3 is squared, giving 9, and then the minus sign is applied, giving minus 9.
This catches out many people, and even some calculators disagree with each other. The brackets settle it.
?? What is open bracket minus 2, close bracket, cubed? Cubed means multiply three of them together.
=> Minus 2 times minus 2 is plus 4. Plus 4 times minus 2 is minus 8. So the answer is minus 8.
## Job four: function notation

Here is a use of round brackets that looks like multiplication but is not. In algebra, a function is like a machine that takes a number in and gives a number out. If the machine is called f, then what comes out when you put x in is written f, open bracket, x, close bracket. It is said: f of x.

That was: f of x equals 2 x plus 1. This app says f of x, rather than reading the brackets aloud, because that is how mathematicians say it. The brackets here do not mean multiply. They mean: feed this into the machine.
So f of 3 means put 3 into the machine: 2 times 3 is 6, plus 1 is 7.
?? With the same machine, what is f of 10?
=> Two times 10 is 20, plus 1 is 21.
## Job five: coordinates and lists
Finally, round brackets hold coordinates, pairs of numbers describing a position, like a grid reference on a map.
That was: open bracket, 3, 5, close bracket. It means the point 3 across and 5 up. The comma separates the two numbers, and the brackets keep the pair together as one point.

So round brackets have several jobs: do this first, multiply, keep a negative together, feed a function, and hold a pair. The good news is that the job is almost always clear from what surrounds them. In the next part, we meet the round bracket's relatives: square brackets and curly braces.

Sometimes a parcel contains another parcel. In mathematics, brackets can sit inside other brackets. This is called nesting, like a set of Russian dolls, or like a bird's nest inside a tree inside a forest.
## Working from the inside out
When brackets are nested, the rule is simple. Start with the innermost brackets and work outwards. Listen to this one.
That was: 2 times, open bracket, 3 plus, open bracket, level two, 4 minus 1, close bracket, level two, close bracket.

The words level two tell you that the inner bracket is a second layer inside the first. With the tones on, you will also have heard that the inner bracket's tones were higher in pitch. Deeper means higher, as if climbing a staircase inside the outer parcel.
Now work from the inside out. The innermost bracket is 4 minus 1, which is 3. Now the outer bracket is 3 plus 3, which is 6. Finally, 2 times 6 is 12.
?? Try this: open bracket, 10 minus, open bracket, level two, 2 plus 3, close bracket, level two, close bracket, times 2.
=> Innermost first: 2 plus 3 is 5. Then the outer bracket: 10 minus 5 is 5. Then 5 times 2 is 10.
## Square brackets

When many round brackets are nested, it becomes hard to see which closing bracket belongs to which opening bracket. So writers often change the shape for the outer layers. Square brackets have straight sides and square corners. They do exactly the same job as round brackets. They just make the layers easier to tell apart.
Let us hear the square bracket tones. They have a woodier, slightly lower sound than the round ones. Opening rises, closing falls, as always.
⟦\tone{square-open}⟧ ⟦\tone{square-close}⟧
Here is a formula using them.

That was: 3 times, open square bracket, 2 plus, open bracket, level two, 5 minus 1, close bracket, level two, close square bracket. Inside out: 5 minus 1 is 4. Then 2 plus 4 is 6. Then 3 times 6 is 18.
## Curly braces
For a third layer, writers sometimes use curly braces. Curly braces are wavy, with a little point in the middle of each side. Their tone is bright and bell-like.
⟦\tone{curly-open}⟧ ⟦\tone{curly-close}⟧
In arithmetic, curly braces are just a third style of grouping, used as the outermost layer.

That was a three-layer formula. Let us unwrap it from the inside. The round bracket: 3 plus 2 is 5. The square bracket: 1 plus 5 is 6. The curly brace: 2 times 6 is 12. Finally, outside all of them, 12 minus 5 is 7.
?? Which layer did you work out first, and which last?
=> First the innermost, the round bracket. Then the square bracket around it. Then the curly brace. Last of all, the subtraction outside everything.
In more advanced mathematics, curly braces have a special job of their own, which is holding sets. That is the subject of part five.
## Hearing depth

In this app, nesting depth is shown in three ways. In words, the inner brackets say level two, level three and so on. In tones, each deeper level sounds a little higher, rising by a step called a minor third. And if you choose stereo in Voice and settings, deeper levels also move from side to side, left, then right, so that you can hear the layers spread out around your head. That works best with headphones.
## A matching tip

To check that brackets are balanced, count as you listen. Add one each time a bracket opens and take one away each time one closes. You should finish at zero. If you ever finish above zero, a bracket was left open. Mathematicians do the same thing in their heads, and computer programs check brackets in exactly this way.
?? Count along: open, open, close, open, close, close. Do you end at zero?
=> One, two, one, two, one, zero. Yes, balanced.
So far, curly braces have been a third style of grouping. But in modern mathematics they have a much more important job. Curly braces hold sets.
## What is a set?

A set is simply a collection of things. The things are called its elements, or members. The set of days of the weekend has two elements, Saturday and Sunday. The set of primary colours of light has three: red, green and blue.
When a set is written down, its elements are listed between curly braces, separated by commas.

That was: open curly brace, 1, 2, 3, close curly brace. It is the set containing the numbers 1, 2 and 3. Notice the bell-like tones of the curly braces, marking the edges of the set, like a fence around a field.
## Two rules of sets

Sets have two simple rules. First, order does not matter. The set 1, 2, 3 is exactly the same set as 3, 1, 2. A set is like a bag of shopping, not a queue. Second, nothing is counted twice. The set containing 1, 1 and 2 is just the set containing 1 and 2. Either something is in the bag or it is not.
?? How many elements does the set containing a, b, a, c have?
=> Three: a, b and c. The second a is the same element and is not counted again.
## Belonging
To say that something is an element of a set, mathematicians use a symbol that looks like a rounded letter E. It is said: is an element of, or is in.
That was: 2 is an element of, open curly brace, 1, 2, 3, close curly brace. In plain words, 2 is in the set. It is true.
## The empty set

There is a set with nothing in it, called the empty set. It is like an empty bag. It can be written as two curly braces with nothing between them, or with a special symbol, a circle with a line through it.
That was: open curly brace, close curly brace. The empty set.
## Describing a set by a rule

Listing works for small sets. But what about the set of all positive numbers? There are infinitely many, so we cannot list them. Instead we describe the set by a rule. This is called set-builder notation, and it is one of the places where curly braces really shine.

That was: open curly brace, x, such that, x is greater than 0, close curly brace. In plain words: the set of all numbers x such that x is greater than zero. In other words, all the positive numbers. The little mark in the middle, which on paper is a colon or a vertical line, is said: such that.
Here is a slightly richer one.
⟦\{n\in \mathbb{N} : n<5\}⟧

That was: the set of n in the natural numbers, such that n is less than 5. The natural numbers are the counting numbers. So this set is 1, 2, 3 and 4. Some mathematicians count 0 as a natural number too, in which case 0 joins the set as well. Mathematicians genuinely disagree about this, so books usually say which they mean.
?? Describe in words the set: open curly brace, x, such that, x is an even number less than 10, close curly brace. Can you list it?
=> It is the set of even numbers less than 10. If we start from 2, it is 2, 4, 6 and 8. If we count 0 as even, which mathematicians do, then 0 joins too.
## Combining sets

Two sets can be combined. The union of two sets is everything in either one. The intersection is only what is in both. If one set is your friends who like tea, and another is your friends who like coffee, the union is everyone who likes either, and the intersection is the friends who like both.
That was: the set 1, 2, 3, union the set 3, 4, equals the set 1, 2, 3, 4. Notice the 3 appears only once in the answer, because sets do not count twice.
?? What is the intersection of the set 1, 2, 3 and the set 2, 3, 4?
=> Only the elements in both: the set containing 2 and 3.

Sets are the foundation on which almost all of modern mathematics is built. There is a whole section on sets, logic and proof, if you want to go further. For now, just remember: when you hear the bright bell of a curly brace in an advanced formula, a set is usually nearby.

In algebra, letters stand for numbers we do not know yet, or for any number at all. When a letter is inside a bracket, we cannot simply work out the bracket first, because we do not know what the letter is. Instead, we can open the bracket up. This is called expanding, or multiplying out.
## The idea: everyone gets a share

Imagine you are buying three gift bags for three friends. Each bag contains a book and two chocolates. How many books and chocolates do you need altogether? Three books, and three lots of two chocolates, which is six chocolates.
That is exactly what expanding a bracket does. Write a book as b and a chocolate as c. One bag is b plus 2c. Three bags are three times that bag.

That was: 3, open bracket, b plus 2 c, close bracket, equals 3 b plus 6 c. In plain words, the 3 outside the bracket multiplies everything inside. Every item in the bag gets multiplied by 3, not just the first.
## The rule

The number outside a bracket multiplies every term inside it. This rule has a grand name: the distributive law. The number outside is distributed, shared out, to each term inside, like a postman delivering to every house on a street.
⟦a(b+c)=ab+ac⟧
That was: A, open bracket, b plus c, close bracket, equals A b plus A c.
?? Expand 5, open bracket, x plus 4, close bracket.
=> Five times x is 5 x. Five times 4 is 20. So the answer is 5 x plus 20.
## A check with numbers

You can always check algebra by putting in a number. Let x be 1. Then 5, open bracket, 1 plus 4, close bracket, is 5 times 5, which is 25. And 5 x plus 20 is 5 plus 20, which is also 25. They agree. That is a good habit, and it makes algebra much less frightening: you can always test it.
## Minus signs outside a bracket
Be careful when there is a minus sign outside. It multiplies every term inside too, and that flips their signs.

That was: minus 2, open bracket, x minus 3, close bracket, equals minus 2 x plus 6. The minus 2 times x is minus 2 x. And minus 2 times minus 3 is plus 6, because two negatives make a positive. Forgetting to flip the second sign is the single most common mistake in school algebra.
?? Expand minus, open bracket, x plus 7, close bracket. A lone minus sign in front means minus 1 times the bracket.
=> Minus 1 times x is minus x. Minus 1 times 7 is minus 7. So the answer is minus x minus 7.
## Two brackets multiplied together
Now for the next step: two brackets side by side, which means multiply them.

That was: open bracket, x plus 2, close bracket, open bracket, x plus 3, close bracket. Here every term in the first bracket must multiply every term in the second. Think of a handshake party: each guest from the first group shakes hands with each guest from the second group. There are two guests in each group, so four handshakes.
First, x times x is x squared. Then x times 3 is 3 x. Then 2 times x is 2 x. Then 2 times 3 is 6. Add them up, and the two middle terms combine: 3 x plus 2 x is 5 x.
That was: equals x squared plus 5 x plus 6.
Some teachers call this FOIL: First, Outside, Inside, Last. Others draw a grid. By ear, the handshake picture works well: everyone in the first bracket meets everyone in the second.
?? Expand open bracket, x plus 1, close bracket, open bracket, x plus 4, close bracket. Take your time.
=> The four handshakes: x times x is x squared, x times 4 is 4 x, 1 times x is x, 1 times 4 is 4. Combine the middle: 4 x plus x is 5 x. Answer: x squared plus 5 x plus 4.
## Picturing it as area

There is a lovely way to feel why this works. Imagine a rectangular garden, x plus 2 metres long and x plus 3 metres wide. Its area is the length times the width. Now imagine dividing the garden into four plots: a square plot x by x, a strip x by 3, a strip 2 by x, and a little corner 2 by 3. The four plots together make the whole garden, so the four areas add up to the total. Expanding brackets is just adding up the plots.
In the next part, we go the other way: putting things back into brackets, which is called factorising.

If expanding is unpacking the gift bags, factorising is packing them up again. You start with a long expression and try to write it as something times a bracket. It is like noticing that a pile of items could be shared out into identical bags.
## A common factor
Look at this expression.

That was: 6 x plus 15. Is there a number that divides both 6 x and 15 exactly? Six is 3 times 2, and 15 is 3 times 5. So 3 goes into both. We call 3 a common factor. Take it outside a bracket, and put what is left inside.
That was: 6 x plus 15 equals 3, open bracket, 2 x plus 5, close bracket.
The check is easy: expand the answer. 3 times 2 x is 6 x. 3 times 5 is 15. We are back where we started. Factorising and expanding are opposites, like tying and untying a knot.
?? Factorise 4x plus 8.
=> Four divides both. 4 x is 4 times x, and 8 is 4 times 2. So the answer is 4, open bracket, x plus 2, close bracket.
## Letters can be common factors too
That was: x squared plus 7 x. Both terms contain an x. x squared is x times x, and 7 x is 7 times x. Take the x outside.
That was: equals x, open bracket, x plus 7, close bracket.
?? Factorise 5 x squared plus 10 x. Look for both a number and a letter.
=> Five divides both, and x is in both, so 5 x is a common factor. Five x squared is 5 x times x, and 10 x is 5 x times 2. The answer is 5 x, open bracket, x plus 2, close bracket.
## Factorising into two brackets
In part six, we expanded open bracket x plus 2, close bracket, times open bracket x plus 3, close bracket, and got x squared plus 5 x plus 6. Now let us go backwards. Suppose we are given:

We want two brackets, each of the form x plus something. Remember the handshakes. The last term, 6, came from multiplying the two numbers together. The middle term, 5 x, came from adding the two numbers together. So we need two numbers that multiply to make 6 and add to make 5.
?? Think: which two numbers multiply to 6 and add to 5?
=> 2 and 3. Two times three is six, and two plus three is five.
So the answer is:

Let us try another. x squared plus 7 x plus 12. We need two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7. The pairs that multiply to 12 are 1 and 12, 2 and 6, and 3 and 4. Only 3 and 4 add to 7. So the answer is open bracket x plus 3, close bracket, open bracket x plus 4, close bracket.
?? Factorise x squared plus 6 x plus 8.
=> Multiply to 8 and add to 6: 2 and 4. The answer is open bracket x plus 2, close bracket, open bracket x plus 4, close bracket.
## The difference of two squares
One pattern is so beautiful that it is worth knowing by heart.

That was: x squared minus 9 equals open bracket x plus 3, close bracket, open bracket x minus 3, close bracket. In plain words, a square minus another square always factorises into a plus bracket and a minus bracket. When you expand, the plus 3 x and minus 3 x cancel each other out, leaving only x squared minus 9.

It gives a wonderful mental arithmetic trick. What is 21 times 19? That is open bracket 20 plus 1, close bracket, times open bracket 20 minus 1, close bracket, which is 20 squared minus 1 squared, which is 400 minus 1, which is 399.
?? Use the same trick for 31 times 29.
=> That is 30 plus 1 times 30 minus 1, which is 900 minus 1, which is 899.
## Why factorise?

Factorising is not just a school exercise. It is how equations are solved, which you will hear about in the algebra section. If two things multiplied together make zero, then one of them must be zero. So if open bracket x plus 2, close bracket, times open bracket x plus 3, close bracket, equals zero, then x must be minus 2 or minus 3. Packing an expression into brackets often reveals its secrets.

Here is a use of brackets that surprises many people, because the brackets do not have to match. An opening square bracket can be closed by a round bracket. This happens in interval notation, which is a short way of describing a stretch of the number line.
## Stretches of the number line

Picture the number line again, as a long road. An interval is a stretch of that road between two points, say from 2 to 5. But there is a question. Are the end points themselves included? Is 5 in the stretch, or does the stretch stop just short of 5?
Think of a car park that is open from 8 o'clock until 6 o'clock. Can you arrive at exactly 6? It depends on the rules. Interval notation answers that question with the shape of the bracket.
## Square means in, round means out
A square bracket means the end point is included. A round bracket means the end point is left out.
A helpful picture: the square bracket has corners that grip the number tightly, like a hand closing around it. The round bracket curves away from the number, as if shying away, not quite touching.
That was: open square bracket, 2, 5, close square bracket. All the numbers from 2 to 5, including both 2 and 5. This is called a closed interval.

That was: open bracket, 2, 5, close bracket. All the numbers between 2 and 5, but not 2 or 5 themselves. It includes 2.1, and 4.999, but not 5. This is called an open interval. Notice that with round brackets on both sides, it sounds just like a coordinate point. In practice, the surrounding words always tell you which is meant.
## Mixed brackets
Now the surprising part.

That was: open square bracket, 0, 1, close bracket. Listen to the tones: a square bracket's woody tone opened it, but a round bracket's tone closed it. This is all the numbers from 0 up to, but not including, 1. Zero is in. One is out. This is called a half-open interval.
?? Is 0.5 in that interval? Is 0? Is 1?
=> 0.5 is in, because it is between 0 and 1. 0 is in, because of the square bracket. 1 is out, because of the round bracket.

Here is a real-life example. A child's ticket is for ages from 0 up to, but not including, 16. On your sixteenth birthday you need an adult ticket. In interval notation, the child's age range is open square bracket 0, 16, close round bracket.
?? Describe in interval notation the temperatures from minus 5 to 10 degrees, including minus 5 but not including 10.
=> Open square bracket, minus 5, 10, close round bracket. Square at minus 5 because it is included, round at 10 because it is not.
## Infinity always gets a round bracket
Some intervals go on forever. All the numbers bigger than 3 stretch away towards infinity.
⟦(3, \infty)⟧

That was: open bracket, 3, infinity, close bracket. Infinity is not a number you can reach or include, so it always gets a round bracket, the shy one. And here the round bracket at 3 means 3 itself is not included: only numbers strictly bigger than 3.
## Interval notation and inequalities

Intervals can also be described with inequality signs, which you will meet in algebra. The interval open square bracket 0, 1, close round bracket can also be said: 0 is less than or equal to x, and x is less than 1.
That was: 0 is less than or equal to x, which is less than 1. The or equal to matches the square bracket. The strict less than matches the round bracket.
?? Translate into interval notation: x is greater than 2 and less than or equal to 7.
=> Round bracket at 2, because 2 is not included, and square bracket at 7, because 7 is. Open bracket, 2, 7, close square bracket.

Not every country uses this notation the same way. In France, for example, mathematicians write a reversed square bracket instead of a round one. But in Britain and America, square for in and round for out is the standard, and it is worth knowing when you meet it in an article.
Even confident mathematicians slip up with brackets now and then. In this part, we will gather the most common confusions in one place, so that you can recognise them when they appear.
## Confusion one: squaring a bracket
This is the most famous mistake in all of school algebra.

That was: open bracket, A plus b, close bracket, squared. Many people expect it to equal A squared plus b squared. It does not. Squaring means multiplying the bracket by itself, so every term meets every term, as in the handshake picture from part six.
That was: equals A squared plus 2 A b plus b squared. The middle term, 2 A b, is the part people forget.

In mathematics and computer programming, the order of operations is a collection of conventions about which arithmetic operations to perform first in order to evaluate a given mathematical expression.

These conventions are formalized with a ranking of the operations. The rank of an operation is called its precedence, and an operation with a higher precedence is performed before operations with lower precedence. Calculators generally perform operations with the same precedence from left to right, but some programming languages and calculators adopt different conventions.
A formula is omitted here.

For example, multiplication is granted a higher precedence than addition, and it has been this way since the introduction of modern algebraic notation. When exponents were introduced in the 16th and 17th centuries, they were given precedence over both addition and multiplication and placed as a superscript to the right of their base.

These conventions exist to avoid notational ambiguity while allowing notation to remain brief and uncluttered. Where it is desired to override the precedence conventions, or even simply to emphasize them, parentheses can be used. If multiple pairs of parentheses are required in a mathematical expression (such as in the case of nested parentheses), the parentheses may be replaced by other types of brackets to avoid confusion, as in [2 × (3 + 4)] − 5 = 9.

These conventions are meaningful only when the usual notation (called infix notation) is used. When functional or Polish notation is used for all operations, the order of operations results from the notation itself.
## Conventional order

The order of operations, that is, the order in which the operations in an expression are usually performed, results from a convention adopted throughout mathematics, science, technology, and many computer programming languages. It is summarized as:
Parentheses; Exponentiation; Multiplication and division; Addition and subtraction.

This means that to evaluate an expression, one first evaluates any sub-expression inside parentheses, working from inside to outside if there is more than one set. Whether inside parentheses or not, the operation that is higher in the above list should be applied first. Operations of the same precedence are conventionally evaluated from left to right.

If each division is replaced with multiplication by the reciprocal (multiplicative inverse), then the associative and commutative laws of multiplication allow the factors in each term to be multiplied together in any order. Sometimes multiplication and division are given equal precedence, or sometimes multiplication is given higher precedence than division; see § Mixed division and multiplication below. If each subtraction is replaced with the addition of the opposite (additive inverse), then the associative and commutative laws of addition allow terms to be added in any order.

The radical symbol ⟦√⟧, which signifies a square root, is traditionally extended by a bar (the vinculum) over the radicand; this avoids the need for parentheses around the radicand. Other functions use parentheses around the input to avoid ambiguity. The parentheses can be omitted if the input is a single numerical variable or constant, as in the case of ⟦sin x = sin(x)⟧ and ⟦sin π = sin(π)⟧. Traditionally this convention extends to monomials; thus, ⟦sin 3x = sin(3x)⟧ and even a long formula, but ⟦sin x + y = sin(x) + y⟧, because ⟦x + y⟧ is not a monomial. However, this convention is not universally understood, and some authors prefer explicit parentheses. Some calculators and programming languages require parentheses around function inputs, while others do not.
Parentheses and alternate symbols of grouping can be used to override the usual order of operations or to make the intended order explicit. Grouped symbols can be treated as a single expression.

## Mixed division and multiplication

There is no universal convention for interpreting an expression containing both division denoted by '÷' and multiplication denoted by '×'. Proposed conventions include assigning the operations equal precedence and evaluating them from left to right, or equivalently treating division as multiplication by the reciprocal and then evaluating in any order; evaluating all multiplications first followed by divisions from left to right; or eschewing such expressions and instead always disambiguating them by explicit parentheses.

Beyond primary education, the symbol '÷' for division is seldom used, but is replaced by the use of algebraic fractions. These are most explicitly and unambiguously written "vertically" with the numerator stacked above the denominator separated by a fraction bar. But they can also be written "horizontally" with the numerator and denominator separated by the slash symbol '/'. That is, expressions such as ⟦a ÷ b⟧ are avoided in favor of ⟦⁠a/b⁠⟧ or ⟦a / b⟧.

Multiplication denoted by juxtaposition (also known as implied multiplication) creates a visual unit and is often given higher precedence than most other operations. In academic literature, when inline fractions are combined with implied multiplication without explicit parentheses, the multiplication is conventionally interpreted as having higher precedence than division, so that, for example 1 / 2n is interpreted to mean 1 / (2 · n) rather than (1 / 2) · n. ## Mnemonics

Mnemonic acronyms are often taught in primary schools to help students remember the order of operations. The acronym PEMDAS, which stands for Parentheses, Exponents, Multiplication/Division, Addition/Subtraction, is common in the United States and France. Sometimes the letters are expanded into words of a mnemonic sentence such as "Please Excuse My Dear Aunt Sally". The United Kingdom and other Commonwealth countries may use BODMAS (or sometimes BOMDAS), standing for Brackets, Of, Division/Multiplication, Addition/Subtraction, with "of" meaning fraction multiplication. Sometimes the O is instead expanded as Order, meaning exponent or root, or replaced by I for Indices in the alternative mnemonic BIDMAS. In Canada and New Zealand BEDMAS is common.

These mnemonics may be misleading when written this way. For example, misinterpreting any of the above rules to mean "addition first, subtraction afterward" would incorrectly evaluate the expression ⟦a − b + c⟧ as ⟦a − ( b + c )⟧, while the correct evaluation is ⟦( a − b ) + c⟧. These values are different when ⟦c ≠ 0⟧.

In Germany, the convention is simply taught as Punktrechnung vor Strichrechnung, "dot operations before line operations" referring to the graphical shapes of the symbols · (multiplication), ∶ (division), + (addition), and − (subtraction). This avoids the potential for the above misunderstanding.

Mnemonic acronyms have been criticized for not developing a conceptual understanding of the order of operations and not addressing students' questions about its purpose or flexibility. Students learning the order of operations via mnemonic acronyms routinely make mistakes, as do some pre-service teachers. Even when students correctly learn the acronym, a disproportionate focus on memorization of trivia crowds out substantive mathematical content. The acronym's procedural application does not match experts' intuitive understanding of mathematical notation: mathematical notation indicates groupings in ways other than parentheses or brackets and a mathematical expression is a tree-like hierarchy rather than a linearly "ordered" structure; furthermore, there is no single order by which mathematical expressions must be simplified or evaluated and no universal canonical simplification for any particular expression, and experts fluently apply valid transformations and substitutions in whatever order is convenient, so learning a rigid procedure can lead students to a misleading and limiting understanding of mathematical notation.
## Calculators

Different calculators follow different orders of operations. Many simple calculators without a stack implement chain input, working in button-press order without any priority given to different operations, give a different result from that given by more sophisticated calculators.

Calculators may associate exponents to the left or to the right. For example, the expression a^b^c is interpreted as a on the TI-92 and the TI-30XS MultiView in "Mathprint mode", whereas it is interpreted as (⟦a^{b}⟧) on the TI-30XII and the TI-30XS MultiView in "Classic mode".

An expression like 1/2x is interpreted as 1/(2x) by TI-82, as well as many modern Casio calculators (configurable on some like the fx-9750GIII), but as (1/2)x by TI-83 and every other TI calculator released since 1996, as well as by all Hewlett-Packard calculators with algebraic notation. While the first interpretation may be expected by some users due to the nature of implied multiplication, the latter is more in line with the rule that multiplication and division are of equal precedence.
When the user is unsure how a calculator will interpret an expression, parentheses can be used to remove the ambiguity.

Order of operations arose due to the adaptation of infix notation in standard mathematical notation, which can be notationally ambiguous without such conventions, as opposed to postfix notation or prefix notation, which do not need orders of operations. Hence, calculators utilizing reverse Polish notation (RPN) using a stack to enter expressions in the correct order of precedence do not need parentheses or any model-specific order of execution.
## Programming languages

Most programming languages use precedence levels that conform to the order commonly used in mathematics, though others, such as APL and Smalltalk, have no operator precedence rules (in APL, evaluation is strictly right to left; in Smalltalk, it is strictly left to right).

## History

The order of operations emerged progressively over centuries. The rule that multiplication has precedence over addition was incorporated into the development of algebraic notation in the 1600s, since the distributive property implies this as a natural hierarchy. As recently as the 1920s, the historian of mathematics Florian Cajori identifies disagreement about whether multiplication should have precedence over division, or whether they should be treated equally. The term "order of operations" and the "PEMDAS/BEDMAS" mnemonics were formalized only in the late 19th or early 20th century, as demand for standardized textbooks grew.

Ambiguity about issues such as whether implicit multiplication takes precedence over explicit multiplication and division in such expressions as a/2b, which could be interpreted as a/(2b) or (a/2) × b, implies that the conventions are not yet completely stable.

In mathematics, brackets of various typographical forms, such as parentheses, square brackets [ ], braces ⟦\{\}⟧ and angle brackets, are frequently used in mathematical notation. Generally, such bracketing denotes some form of grouping: in evaluating an expression containing a bracketed sub-expression, the operators in the sub-expression take precedence over those surrounding it. Sometimes, for the clarity of reading, different kinds of brackets are used to express the same meaning of precedence in a single expression with deep nesting of sub-expressions.

Historically, other notations, such as the vinculum, were similarly used for grouping. In present-day use, these notations all have specific meanings. The earliest use of brackets to indicate aggregation (that is grouping) was suggested in 1608 by Christopher Clavius, and in 1629 by Albert Girard.

Given a set ⟦S⟧ and two binary operators ⟦∗⟧ and ⟦+⟧ on ⟦S ,⟧
the operation ⟦∗⟧ is left-distributive over (or with respect to) ⟦+⟧ if, given any elements ⟦x , y , \text{ and } z⟧ of ⟦S ,⟧
the operation ⟦∗⟧ is right-distributive over ⟦+⟧ if, given any elements ⟦x , y , \text{ and } z⟧ of ⟦S ,⟧
and the operation ⟦∗⟧ is distributive over ⟦+⟧ if it is left- and right-distributive.
When ⟦∗⟧ is commutative, the three conditions above are logically equivalent.

The operators used for examples in this section are those of the usual addition ⟦+⟧ and multiplication ⟦⋅ .⟧
If the operation denoted ⟦⋅⟧ is not commutative, there is a distinction between left-distributivity and right-distributivity:
$$ a ⋅ ( b ± c ) = a ⋅ b ± a ⋅ c \text{ (left-distributive) }
$$ ( a ± b ) ⋅ c = a ⋅ c ± b ⋅ c \text{ (right-distributive) }
In either case, the distributive property can be described in words as:
To multiply a sum (or difference) by a factor, each summand (or minuend and subtrahend) is multiplied by this factor and the resulting products are added (or subtracted).

If the operation outside the parentheses (in this case, the multiplication) is commutative, then left-distributivity implies right-distributivity and vice versa, and one talks simply of distributivity.
One example of an operation that is "only" right-distributive is division, which is not commutative:

In this case, left-distributivity does not apply:

The distributive laws are among the axioms for rings (like the ring of integers) and fields (like the field of rational numbers). Here multiplication is distributive over addition, but addition is not distributive over multiplication. Examples of structures with two operations that are each distributive over the other are Boolean algebras such as the algebra of sets or the switching algebra.

Multiplying sums can be put into words as follows: When a sum is multiplied by a sum, multiply each summand of a sum with each summand of the other sum (keeping track of signs) then add up all of the resulting products.

## Distributivity and rounding

In approximate arithmetic, such as floating-point arithmetic, the distributive property of multiplication (and division) over addition may fail because of the limitations of arithmetic precision. For example, the identity ⟦1 / 3 + 1 / 3 + 1 / 3 = ( 1 + 1 + 1 ) / 3⟧ fails in decimal arithmetic, regardless of the number of significant digits. In mathematics, an interval is the set of all real numbers lying between two fixed lower or upper bounds ("endpoints" or boundary points) with no "gaps". For example, the set of real numbers consisting of ⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧, and all numbers in between is an interval, denoted ⟦[0, 1]⟧ and called the unit interval. An interval may contain neither endpoint (called an open interval), both endpoints (called a closed interval), or either endpoint (called a semi-open or semi-closed interval).

The intervals just described are the bounded intervals. Often intervals are also allowed to extend without bound in one or both directions, with the unbounded side being denoted by a positive or negative infinity symbol. The set of all positive real numbers is an interval in this sense, denoted ⟦(0, ∞)⟧; the set of all real numbers is an interval that is unbounded on both ends, denoted ⟦(-∞, ∞)⟧.

Intervals are ubiquitous in mathematical analysis. For example, they occur implicitly in the epsilon-delta definition of continuity; the intermediate value theorem asserts that the image of an interval by a continuous function is an interval; integrals of real functions are defined over an interval; and so on For example, interval arithmetic consists of computing with intervals instead of real numbers for providing a guaranteed enclosure of the result of a numerical computation, even in the presence of uncertainties of input data and rounding errors.
Intervals can be defined more generally on any totally ordered set, such as integers or rational numbers. The notation of integer intervals is considered in the special section below.
## Definition of an interval

An interval is a subset of the real numbers that contains all real numbers lying between any two numbers of the subset. Examples are the numbers ⟦x⟧ from one to two, ⟦1 ≤ x ≤ 2⟧, and the numbers ⟦y⟧ greater than 10, that is ⟦y > 10⟧. Under this definition, the empty set and the entire set of real numbers are both intervals.

The endpoints of an interval are its supremum (least upper bound), and its infimum (greatest lower bound), if they exist as real numbers. If the infimum does not exist and the interval is not empty, one says often that the corresponding endpoint is negative infinity, written ⟦− ∞ .⟧ Similarly, if the supremum of a non-empty interval does not exist, one says that the corresponding endpoint is positive infinity, written ⟦+ ∞ .⟧

Non-empty intervals are completely determined by their endpoints and whether each endpoint belongs to the interval. This is a consequence of the least-upper-bound property of the real numbers, which implies that if the elements of a non-empty interval are all less than some finite value, then the interval has a supremum. This characterization is used to specify intervals by means of interval notation, where a square or rounded bracket (parenthesis) indicates whether or not an endpoint belongs to the interval.

## Degenerate intervals

A degenerate interval is any set consisting of a single real number (that is an interval of the form ⟦[a, a]⟧). Some authors include the empty set in this definition. A real interval that is neither empty nor degenerate is said to be proper, and has infinitely many elements.
## Bounded intervals

An interval is said to be left-bounded or right-bounded, if there is some real number that is, respectively, smaller than or larger than all its elements. An interval is said to be bounded, if it is both left- and right-bounded; and is said to be unbounded otherwise. Intervals that are bounded at only one end are said to be half-bounded. The empty set is bounded, and the set of all reals is the only interval that is unbounded at both ends. Bounded intervals are also commonly known as finite intervals.

Bounded intervals are bounded sets, in the sense that their diameter (which is equal to the absolute difference between the endpoints) is finite. The diameter may be called the length, width, measure, range, or size of the interval. The size of unbounded intervals is usually defined as ⟦+∞⟧, and the size of the empty interval may be defined as ⟦0⟧ (or left undefined).
The centre (midpoint) of a bounded interval with endpoints ⟦a⟧ and ⟦b⟧ is ⟦(a + b)/2⟧, and its radius is the half-length ⟦|a - b|/2⟧. These concepts are undefined for empty or unbounded intervals.
## Categorisation by minimum and maximum elements

An interval is said to be left-open if and only if it contains no minimum (an element that is smaller than all other elements); right-open if it contains no maximum; and open if it contains neither. The set of non-negative reals is a closed interval that is right-open but not left-open.

An interval is said to be left-closed if it has a minimum element or is left-unbounded, right-closed if it has a maximum or is right unbounded; it is simply closed if it is both left-closed and right closed.
## Sub-intervals and related constructions
An interval ⟦I⟧ is a subinterval of interval ⟦J⟧ if ⟦I⟧ is a subset of ⟦J⟧. An interval ⟦I⟧ is a proper subinterval of ⟦J⟧ if ⟦I⟧ is a proper subset of ⟦J⟧.

The interior of an interval ⟦I⟧ is the largest open interval that is contained in ⟦I⟧; it is also the set of points in ⟦I⟧ which are not endpoints of ⟦I⟧. The closure of ⟦I⟧ is the smallest closed interval that contains ⟦I⟧; which is also the set ⟦I⟧ augmented with its finite endpoints.
For any set ⟦X⟧ of real numbers, the interval enclosure or interval span of ⟦X⟧ is the unique interval that contains ⟦X⟧, and does not properly contain any other interval that also contains ⟦X⟧.

## Dyadic intervals

A dyadic interval is a bounded real interval whose endpoints are ⟦\frac{j}{2^{n}}⟧ and ⟦\frac{j + 1}{2^{n}} ,⟧ where ⟦j⟧ and ⟦n⟧ are integers. Depending on the context, either endpoint may or may not be included in the interval.
Dyadic intervals have the following properties:
The length of a dyadic interval is always an integer power of two.
Each dyadic interval is contained in exactly one dyadic interval of twice the length.
Each dyadic interval is spanned by two dyadic intervals of half the length.
If two open dyadic intervals overlap, then one of them is a subset of the other.
The dyadic intervals consequently have a structure that reflects that of an infinite binary tree.

Dyadic intervals are relevant to several areas of numerical analysis, including adaptive mesh refinement, multigrid methods and wavelet analysis. Another way to represent such a structure is p-adic analysis (for ⟦p = 2⟧).

The intermediate value theorem captures the intuition that if ⟦f : [ a , b ] → ℝ⟧ is a real valued continuous function on an interval ⟦[ a , b ]⟧ and ⟦d⟧ is any value between ⟦f ( a )⟧ and ⟦f ( b )⟧, then we expect to find a value ⟦c⟧ between ⟦a⟧ and ⟦b⟧ where ⟦f ( c ) = d⟧. An equivalent formulation of the theorem asserts that the image of an interval by a continuous function is an interval.
## Confidence intervals

Confidence intervals are important in statistical inference and provide a range of estimated values for an unknown statistical parameter, such as a population mean. Unlike other kinds of interval, a confidence interval is evaluated from a random sample and the interval endpoints are real-valued random variables. A different sample may well give a different result.

When sampling is repeated there is a pre-set probability, known as the confidence level, that a corresponding interval contains the true value of the unknown parameter. For example, if the chosen confidence level were 0.95 and the same sampling procedure were repeated many times, in the long run approximately 95 percent of the resulting intervals would be expected to contain the true value.

The normal distribution provides a simplified illustration. It has a probability density function whose graph is the familiar bell curve. These two parameters distinguish one bell curve from another, but in all cases the region within two standard deviations either side of the mean represents a probability of approximately 0.95. ## Balls

An open finite interval ⟦( a , b )⟧ is a 1-dimensional open ball with a center at ⟦\frac{1}{2} ( a + b )⟧ and a radius of ⟦\frac{1}{2} ( b − a ) .⟧ The closed finite interval ⟦[ a , b ]⟧ is the corresponding closed ball, and the interval's two endpoints ⟦\{ a , b \}⟧ form a 0-dimensional sphere. Generalized to ⟦n⟧-dimensional Euclidean space, a ball is the set of points whose distance from the center is less than the radius. In the 2-dimensional case, a ball is called a disk.

If a half-space is taken as a kind of degenerate ball (without a well-defined center or radius), a half-space can be taken as analogous to a half-bounded interval, with its boundary plane as the (degenerate) sphere corresponding to the finite endpoint.
## Multi-dimensional intervals

A finite interval is (the interior of) a 1-dimensional hyperrectangle. Generalized to real coordinate space ⟦ℝ^{n} ,⟧ an axis-aligned hyperrectangle (or box) is the Cartesian product of ⟦n⟧ finite intervals. For ⟦n = 2⟧ this is a rectangle; for ⟦n = 3⟧ this is a rectangular cuboid (also called a "box").
Allowing for a mix of open, closed, and infinite endpoints, the Cartesian product of any ⟦n⟧ intervals, ⟦I = I_{1} × I_{2} × ⋯ × I_{n}⟧ is sometimes called an ⟦n⟧-dimensional interval.

A facet of such an interval ⟦I⟧ is the result of replacing any non-degenerate interval factor ⟦I_{k}⟧ by a degenerate interval consisting of a finite endpoint of ⟦I_{k} .⟧ The faces of ⟦I⟧ comprise ⟦I⟧ itself and all faces of its facets. The corners of ⟦I⟧ are the faces that consist of a single point of ⟦ℝ^{n} .⟧
## Convex polytopes

Any finite interval can be constructed as the intersection of half-bounded intervals (with an empty intersection taken to mean the whole real line), and the intersection of any number of half-bounded intervals is a (possibly empty) interval. Generalized to ⟦n⟧-dimensional affine space, an intersection of half-spaces (of arbitrary orientation) is (the interior of) a convex polytope, or in the 2-dimensional case a convex polygon.
## Domains
An open interval is a connected open set of real numbers. Generalized to topological spaces in general, a non-empty connected open set is called a domain.
## Complex intervals
Intervals of complex numbers can be defined as regions of the complex plane, either rectangular or circular.

## Topological algebra

Intervals can be associated with points of the plane, and hence regions of intervals can be associated with regions of the plane. Generally, an interval in mathematics corresponds to an ordered pair ⟦(x, y)⟧ taken from the direct product ⟦ℝ × ℝ⟧ of real numbers with itself, where it is often assumed that ⟦y > x⟧. For purposes of mathematical structure, this restriction is discarded, and "reversed intervals" where ⟦y - x < 0⟧ are allowed. Then, the collection of all intervals ⟦[x, y]⟧ can be identified with the topological ring formed by the direct sum of ⟦ℝ⟧ with itself, where addition and multiplication are defined component-wise.

The identity element of this algebra is the condensed interval ⟦[1, 1]⟧. If interval ⟦[x, y]⟧ is not in one of the ideals, then it has multiplicative inverse ⟦[1/x, 1/y]⟧. Endowed with the usual topology, the algebra of intervals forms a topological ring. The group of units of this ring consists of four quadrants determined by the axes, or ideals in this case. The identity component of this group is quadrant I.
